title: Curry Without Crosstalk
statement_md:
Implement `curry(fn)`. It returns a function that collects arguments across calls until it has at least `fn.length` of them, then calls `fn` with **all** the collected arguments, in order, and returns its result. Until then, each call returns a new function that keeps collecting.

Every partially applied function is **independent**. Calling the same partial twice must give two separate continuations: arguments passed to one must never show up in the other.

- A call with no arguments collects nothing and returns a function that behaves the same way.
- If `fn.length` is `0`, the first call runs `fn`.
- Arguments beyond `fn.length` are passed through to `fn`, not dropped.

Functions can't be test-case values, so the judge calls the provided `curryTrace` driver. It curries a function of `arity` parameters that returns its own arguments, and replays `calls`, where each `[from, args]` calls an earlier result: `0` is the curried function, and `i` is the result of call `i`. A call that returns a function is recorded as `"fn"`. Implement `curry` only; don't edit the driver.
constraints: Every `from` refers to an earlier result that is still a function.

solutions.title: A Fresh Closure per Call
solutions.intuition_md:
The tempting version keeps one `args` array and pushes into it on every call. That works for a single chain, and breaks the moment a partial is reused: `add1 = f(1)` followed by `add1(2)` and `add1(3)` would make the second call see `[1, 2, 3]`, because both continuations share one array.

The fix is to treat collected arguments as a *value*, not state. Each call builds a new array (`concat` copies), and either finishes or returns a new closure over that new array. Nothing a closure captures ever changes after it's created, so partials can't interfere.
solutions.algorithm_md: `gather(collected)` returns a function. When called, it computes `args = collected.concat(callArgs)`. If `args.length >= fn.length`, it returns `fn.apply(this, args)`; otherwise it returns `gather(args)`. `curry` returns `gather([])`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Each call copies the arguments collected so far, which is at most $n = $ `fn.length` plus the new ones.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Each live partial holds its own copy of its collected arguments.

solutions.title: Let `bind` Do the Bookkeeping
solutions.intuition_md:
`Function.prototype.bind` already does exactly this job: `g = f.bind(null, a)` is a new function that remembers `a` and prepends it on every call, and it never mutates `f`. It also sets `g.length` to `f.length - 1`, clamped at `0`.

So each call can bind its arguments onto the previous function, and `next.length === 0` means nothing is missing any more: call it. Every bind returns a new function, so independence comes for free.
solutions.algorithm_md: `step(bound)` returns a function. When called with arguments, it computes `next = bound.bind(null, ...arguments)`. If `next.length === 0`, it returns `next()`; otherwise it returns `step(next)`. `curry(fn)` is `step(fn)`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Invoking the final bound function unwinds one layer per `bind`, and there are at most $n$ of them (one per call that added arguments).
solutions.space_complexity_reason: A chain of up to $n$ bound functions, each holding its own arguments.
